name: Pale Mauve
lede: Pale Mauve is a light, soft lilac-purple, the faded end of [[mauve]]'s long fashion career.

sections.title: From display to mourning
sections.body:
Pale Mauve is simply a lightened [[mauve]], the flower-named color made famous by the dye of 1856 [3]. Garfield records that mauve shifted from a showy, frivolous color to a color of mourning [1].

In 1863, before her marriage to the Prince of Wales, Princess Alexandra arrived in London wearing pale mauve poplin cut as half-mourning [1]. Queen Victoria moved from black to mauve within four years of losing Prince Albert [1]. By 1869 the color was nearly forgotten, replaced by another dye craze [1].

The swatch on this page is #D9C8EF, the screen value we hold for it, which is an approximation and not a measured pigment [3]. Like any pale color it sits between its hue and [[white]], and because the name is a description and not a tradition, other lists may place it a little differently [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Pale Mauve is rare in our archive: 3 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.01 percent, as photographed [2]. In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1930s and rose fastest in the 1920s, though Google Books counts every sense of the words [2].
